ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (movement disorders) Consultation — William Shakespeare — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review of tremor tests, diagnosis, alcohol follow-up, and movement disorders neurology consultation

text.paragraph: A 51-year-old right-handed writer with six months of worsening tremor of the writing hand on a background of milder shaking for several years. Please classify the tremor, exclude early Parkinson disease and other causes, and advise on treatment. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two to four weeks. [S]

list.item: What type of tremor is this, by the MDS consensus classification: essential tremor, an enhanced physiological tremor from alcohol or caffeine, or early Parkinson disease?
Is any imaging, such as brain MRI or dopamine transporter scanning, needed?
Do you advise propranolol, and at what dose and titration, or primidone instead?
What can he do to keep writing by hand, and is occupational therapy worthwhile?
How should his drinking, which briefly steadies the tremor, be addressed in the treatment plan?

text.paragraph: Mr. Shakespeare is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Sule, two weeks after his first visit. He describes a slight shake when holding a full cup for three or four years, and over six months a handwriting tremor that makes long drafts tiring and his signature unsteady; he brought a page from ten years ago and one written this morning, which show a clear change. The tremor appears with posture and action, not at rest, in both hands, worse on the right. It is worse with fatigue, coffee, and the morning after drinking, and eases for an hour after a glass of wine. He has no slowness, stiffness, falls, change in voice or facial expression, loss of smell, constipation, or dream enactment, and no head or leg tremor. He takes no medicines or supplements. Since his first visit he has cut his drinking to about 14 drinks a week and his coffee to three cups. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in April 1564; the exact date of his birth is not recorded, although it is most often celebrated on 23 April. His baptism is recorded in the parish register of Holy Trinity Church on Wednesday 26 April 1564 (Julian; 6 May 1564, Gregorian), in Latin, as 'Gulielmus filius Johannes Shakspere'. Baptisms typically took place within three days of birth. [D]

His father, John Shakespeare, was a glover who also traded in wool and lent money, served on the town council, and became high bailiff in 1568. Before William was born his parents had lost two infant daughters, Joan within the first few weeks of her life and Margaret a year after she was born; a younger sister, Anne, died at the age of eight. [D]
At eighteen he married Anne Hathaway of Shottery; their daughter Susanna was born six months after the marriage, followed by the twins Judith and Hamnet in 1585. Hamnet died at the age of eleven. [D]
His wife and children remained in Stratford while he worked in London, and in 1597 he bought New Place, a large house in the centre of the town, which was his family home. [D]

text.paragraph: 6 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

tr.td: Tremor of the writing hand for six months, with shaky, effortful handwriting and spilling from cups; under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem echoing, without asserting, the shaky signatures on his 1616 will (CLM-0006, R); superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.

Essential tremor (MDS 1608 criteria): bilateral upper-limb postural and kinetic tremor, right more than left, for at least three years, worse over six months, without head or voice tremor or other neurological signs; enhanced by alcohol rebound and caffeine; thyroid and metabolic causes excluded

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. The shakiness of his signatures is documented as an interpretation (CLM-0006, R, possible); no tremor is documented in his lifetime, and the mercury hypothesis (CLM-0010) is disputed.
Hazardous drinking (AUDIT 12; about 24 standard drinks a week with heavier evenings with friends), without an alcohol use disorder; raised GGT
S — Synthetic finding. The only historical mention of his drinking is a story written down decades after his death (CLM-0008, R); it is not treated as evidence of his habits.

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1616-01-26; see the referring visit's Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Normal facial expression, blink rate, eye movements, and speech; no voice or head tremor

Postural and kinetic tremor of both hands, right more than left, moderate amplitude, about six to seven beats a second, with no re-emergent tremor after a pause; no rest tremor even with distraction; finger and foot tapping fast without decrement; tone normal without activation; no dystonic posturing
Finger-nose accurate apart from the tremor; tandem gait normal; arm swing symmetrical; pull test normal
TETRAS performance subscale 22 of 64 and activities of daily living subscale 18 of 48; writing item 3; right Archimedes spiral wide and jagged with a clear tremor axis, left mildly irregular

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Essential tremor (G25.0). An isolated tremor syndrome of bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for at least three years, without tremor elsewhere or other neurological signs: essential tremor by the MDS 1608 criteria. Thyroid and metabolic causes are excluded, and he takes no tremor-inducing drug. Alcohol rebound and caffeine add an enhanced physiological component, and the brief response to alcohol is typical of essential tremor. There are no features of Parkinson disease (no rest or re-emergent tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity) or of dystonic tremor, so no imaging is needed. [S]

Hazardous drinking (Z72.89). Alcohol steadies essential tremor for an hour or so and worsens it the next morning; using it as treatment risks escalating use, so it should be discussed openly as part of the tremor plan. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: TSH 1.6 mIU/L; sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 96), glucose 92 mg/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL; ALT 41 U/L, AST 44 U/L, GGT 84 U/L; hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, MCV 99 fL; AUDIT 12; the two handwriting samples; today's vital signs (pulse 78, blood pressure 130/82 mmHg). [S]

list.item: Propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning, increasing after four weeks to 80 mg if the response is partial and the pulse allows, and up to 160 mg a day if needed; check pulse and blood pressure at each visit; do not stop it suddenly. [S]
If propranolol is not tolerated or does not help, primidone starting at 25 mg at night and increased slowly; not both at once for now. [S]
No brain MRI or dopamine transporter scan: the diagnosis is clinical and there are no atypical features. [S]
Occupational therapy for writing: weighted and wide-grip pens, forearm support, slower and larger script, and dictation for long drafts. [S]
Keep drinking within the agreed limits and do not use alcohol to settle the tremor; keep coffee to two cups a day, and avoid decongestants and other stimulants. [S]

TETRAS rating with a handwriting sample and spiral at each treatment review; ask me to see him again if a rest tremor, slowness, imbalance, or head or voice tremor appears, or if two first-line drugs fail, when surgical options would be discussed. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Achterberg-Sule the same day. Mr. Shakespeare was relieved that this is not Parkinson disease and agreed to start propranolol today. [S]
Follow-up: Primary care will titrate propranolol and repeat the tremor rating. I will see him again on request, or in a year to review the course. [S]
